questions.problem: Which of the following gives the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=xy,$ traversed once along the circle $C$ with equation $(x+1)^{2}+{y}^{2}=25?$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a circle of radius $5$ centered at $(-1,0).$ It can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨5\operatorname{cos}⁡t-1,\,5\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,0\le t<2\pi .
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5\operatorname{cos}⁡t-1)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+5\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(5\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{25{sin}^{2}⁡t+25{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{25({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=xy,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(5\operatorname{cos}⁡t-1)(5\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =5\operatorname{sin}⁡t(5\operatorname{cos}⁡t-1).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }5\operatorname{sin}⁡t(5\operatorname{cos}⁡t-1)\cdot 5\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =25{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t(5\operatorname{cos}⁡t-1)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Which of the following gives the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=x+{y}^{2},$ traversed once along the circle $C$ with equation ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=4?$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a circle of radius $2$ centered at $O.$ It can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,2\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,0\le t<2\pi .
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{sin}^{2}⁡t+4{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{4({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=x+{y}^{2},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2} \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+4{sin}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+4{sin}^{2}⁡t)\cdot 2\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+2{sin}^{2}⁡t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Which of the following gives the line integral of the function $f(x,y)={y}^{3},$ traversed once along the circle $C$ with equation $(x-1)^{2}+(y-1)^{2}=36?$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a circle of radius $6$ centered at $(1,1).$ It can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨6\operatorname{cos}⁡t+1,\,6\operatorname{sin}⁡t+1⟩,\,0\le t<2\pi .
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6\operatorname{cos}⁡t+1)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6\operatorname{sin}⁡t+1)j \\  & =-6\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+6\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-6\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(6\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{36{sin}^{2}⁡t+36{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{36({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =6\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)={y}^{3},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(6\operatorname{sin}⁡t+1)^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }((6\operatorname{sin}⁡t+1)^{3})\cdot 6\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =6{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{(6\operatorname{sin}⁡t+1)}^{3}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Which of the following gives the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=1-{y}^{2},$ traversed once along the circle $C$ with equation $(x+3)^{2}+{y}^{2}=1?$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a circle of radius $1$ centered at $(-3,0).$ It can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t-3,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,0\le t<2\pi .
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-3)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=1-{y}^{2},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =1-(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2} \\  & =1-{sin}^{2}⁡t \\  & ={cos}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }({cos}^{2}⁡t)\cdot 1\cdot \text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{cos}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.

$$

$$

$$

We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a circle of radius $3$ centered at $O.$ It can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,3\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{9{sin}^{2}⁡t+9{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{9({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=xy\sqrt{{y}^{2}+1},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\sqrt{(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+1} \\  & =9\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\sqrt{9{sin}^{2}⁡t+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }9\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\sqrt{9{sin}^{2}⁡t+1}\cdot 3\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =27{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\sqrt{9{sin}^{2}⁡t+1}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=9{sin}^{2}⁡t+1,$ $\text{d}u=18\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}27{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\sqrt{9{sin}^{2}⁡t+1}\,\text{d}t & =\frac{3}{2}{\int }_{1}^{1}\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{3}{2}(0) \\  & =0\end{aligned}

questions.problem: Evaluate the line integral of the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-{y}^{2}$ along the circle $C$ with equation ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=16.$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a circle of radius $4$ centered at $O.$ It can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,4\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{16{sin}^{2}⁡t+16{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{16({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-{y}^{2},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}-(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2} \\  & =16{cos}^{2}⁡t-16{sin}^{2}⁡t \\  & =16({cos}^{2}⁡t-{sin}^{2}⁡t) \\  & =16\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }16\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\cdot 4\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =64{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=2t,$ $\text{d}u=2\,\text{d}t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}64{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t & =32{\int }_{0}^{4\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\  & =32\operatorname{sin}⁡u{|}_{0}^{4\pi } \\  & =32(0-0) \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+5\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(5\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{25{sin}^{2}⁡t+25{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{25({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =5\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(5\operatorname{sin}⁡t+1)\cdot 5\,\text{d}t \\  & =5{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(5\operatorname{sin}⁡t+1)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}

canonical_examples.problem: Find, as a definite integral, an expression for the line integral of the function $f(x,y) = x^2-1,$ traversed once along the circle $C$ with equation $x^2 + y^2 = 1.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\int\limits_C f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}s  = \int\limits_a^b  f(\mathbf r(t)) \, \| \mathbf r'(t) \| \, \textrm{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a circle of radius $1$ centered at $O.$ It can be parametrized as 

$$
\mathbf{r}(t) = \big\langle \cos{t}, \: \sin{t} \big\rangle, \qquad 0 \le t \lt 2\pi.
$$

Computing $\mathbf{r}'(t)$ and $\| \mathbf{r}'(t) \|,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y) = x^2-1,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}-1 \\  & ={cos}^{2}⁡t-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }({cos}^{2}⁡t-1)\cdot 1\cdot \text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{cos}^{2}⁡t-1\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

\int\limits_C f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}s  = \int\limits_a^b  f(\mathbf r(t)) \, \| \mathbf r'(t) \| \, \textrm{d}t.

The curve $C$ is a quarter-circle of radius $2$ centered at $O,$ shown below.

$$

Computing $\mathbf{r}'(t)$ and $\| \mathbf{r}'(t) \|,$ we get following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =2\end{aligned}

$$
